1933: Phytic acid chelates iron, zinc and calcium in the intestine and precludes their absorption; a lower content is therefore preferable, since it liberates the very minerals the grain supplies. In popped rice the values ranged from 0.12 in Kalonunia to 0.32% in Kataribhog; the control recorded 0.26%, 6 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalonunia proved the most favourable. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.44% and Kalojira the lowest at 0.20%; against 0.21% for the control, one cultivar exceeded the control, Kalojira being the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.20 and 0.47%, with the control at 0.37%; 5 cultivars exceeded the control, Tulaipanji ranking highest among them. The means are given in Table 4.80 and plotted in Fig. 4.41. All the products exhibited a significant cultivar effect. Significance attached to year in 1 products and to the year × cultivar interaction in 1, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. The coefficient of variation ranged from 2.46 to 6.95%, indicating reliable measurement.
1934: Phytate is deposited as globoids in the aleurone during grain filling and is hydrolysed by endogenous phytase during soaking, so that the residue is contingent upon both processes. Earlier work is concordant. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded that treated brown rice retains approximately half the phytate of untreated grain, and Kumar et al. (2022) demonstrated that reduced phytate corresponds to greater iron and zinc absorption. Bhar et al. (2022) noted that the reduction of phytate constitutes a principal nutritional argument for processed grain, and Hu et al. (2019) concluded that germination and hydrothermal treatment operate by different mechanisms.
1935: No single cultivar proved superior across all the products: Kalojira, Kalonunia and Tulaipanji ranked highest in different ones, so that the decision is contingent upon the product concerned.
1943: Copper is required for iron transport and for several enzymes, cereals constituting a principal dietary source; a higher content in the product is preferable. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in popped rice at 0.51 ppm and Radhatilak the lowest at 0.38 ppm; against 0.51 ppm for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For puffed rice the values lay between 0.29 and 0.62 ppm, with the control at 0.42 ppm; 2 cultivars exceeded the control and Kataribhog ranked first. In flattened rice the values ranged from 0.33 in Radhunipagal to 0.55 ppm in Lal Badshabhog; the control recorded 0.52 ppm, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Lal Badshabhog returned the most favourable value. Table 4.81 gives the means and Fig. 4.42 presents them.
1944: Significance was attained in each of the products. In 3 products the year effect was significant and in 2 the year × cultivar interaction, the cultivars thus retaining a similar order in both years. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation lying between 6.04 and 6.11%. Copper is translocated into the grain by COPT and HMA transporters and sequestered principally in the aleurone, so that cultivars of greater uptake and translocation capacity accumulate more.
1945: Published work is concordant. Sonu et al. (2025) demonstrated that genotype governs grain micronutrient concentration, and Kumar et al. (2022) determined that trace metals are redistributed between bran and endosperm rather than lost. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported that soluble minerals migrate inward from husk and pericarp, and Hu et al. (2019) observed that water movement within the kernel displaces elements from the aleurone. The most favourable entry varied between products: Dudeshwar, Kataribhog and Lal Badshabhog each ranked highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.
1952: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional disorder among rice-eating populations, so that the iron retained in the product is of direct importance; a higher content is preferable. For popped rice the values lay between 2.77 and 3.70 ppm, with the control at 3.10 ppm; here 4 cultivars exceeded the control, Gobindabhog ranking highest. In puffed rice the values ranged from 0.93 in Radhunipagal to 1.76 ppm in Harinakhuri; the control recorded 1.31 ppm, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Harinakhuri returned the most favourable value. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 3.75 ppm and Tulaipanji the lowest at 1.83 ppm; against 2.59 ppm for the control, 3 cultivars exceeded the control, Gobindabhog being the most favourable entry. The values appear in Table 4.82, with Fig. 4.43 presenting the same data. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was determined. The year term was significant in 3 products and the year × cultivar term in 3, so that cultivar ranking held reasonably steady between years. With coefficients of variation of 1.80 to 3.52%, the experiment was well controlled.
1953: Grain iron is contingent upon the quantity remobilised from the flag leaf and upon the chelators effecting its transport, both of which differ between cultivars; cooking translocates a proportion of it inward from the pericarp. The same pattern has been reported previously. Sonu et al. (2025) recorded that grain iron is heritable but that few lines attain nutritional targets, and Kumar et al. (2022) demonstrated that iron migrates inward and becomes more available. Jannasch and Wang (2020) noted that the steep water may convey iron and calcium into the endosperm, and Akter et al. (2025) concluded that iron declined while protein and zinc were concentrated.
1954: The leading cultivar varied with the product, Gobindabhog and Harinakhuri ranking highest in turn, so that no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.
1961: Zinc is required for immune function, growth and wound healing, and after iron is the mineral most frequently deficient in rice-based diets; a higher content is preferable. In popped rice the values ranged from 0.60 in Dudeshwar to 0.79 ppm in Kataribhog; the control recorded 0.60 ppm, 6 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kataribhog returned the most favourable value. Kalojira recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.42 ppm and Lal Badshabhog the lowest at 0.21 ppm; against 0.33 ppm for the control, 5 cultivars exceeded the control, Kalojira being the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.48 and 1.36 ppm, with the control at 0.57 ppm; Gobindabhog ranked first, and 2 cultivars in all exceeded the control. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.83 and illustrated in Fig. 4.44.
1962: Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Year was significant in 3 products and the year × cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. The coefficient of variation remained within 5.21 to 6.38%, indicative of good precision. Zinc loading is contingent upon the HMA2 and HMA4 transporters and upon remobilisation during grain filling, the element being retained in the aleurone largely as phytate salts.
1963: Earlier reports corroborate this finding. Kumar et al. (2022) demonstrated that zinc migrates outward on treatment, unlike iron, and Sonu et al. (2025) determined grain zinc to be polygenic with wide genotypic variance. Hu et al. (2019) reported that zinc is retained in the germ and aleurone, and Oliveira et al. (2026) observed that polishing is of greater consequence than the thermal step. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Kataribhog, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.
1970: Manganese is required by superoxide dismutase and certain other enzymes. The dietary requirement is small, but cereals supply the greater part of it, so that a higher content is preferable. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in popped rice at 0.94 ppm and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.45 ppm; against 0.45 ppm for the control, 8 cultivars exceeded the control, Kalonunia being the most favourable entry. For puffed rice the values lay between 0.18 and 0.45 ppm, with the control at 0.19 ppm; 8 of the cultivars exceeded the control, Gobindabhog ranking highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 0.38 in Lal Badshabhog to 0.84 ppm in Kalonunia; the control recorded 0.43 ppm, 6 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia returned the most favourable value. Table 4.84 carries the means, which are plotted in Fig. 4.45. The cultivars differed significantly in every product. Significance attached to year in 3 products and to the year × cultivar interaction in 1, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 4.30 to 5.96%.
1971: Manganese enters through NRAMP and MTP transporters and accumulates in the aleurone, so that the value is contingent upon uptake and upon the proportion of the outer grain surviving milling. Comparable results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) recorded that aleurone-bound elements are displaced as water redistributes, and Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated that soluble minerals migrate inward during steeping. Sonu et al. (2025) noted that genotype counts for more than environment in mineral density, and Kumar et al. (2022) concluded that retention is contingent upon the initial level and the treatment applied.
1972: Gobindabhog and Kalonunia each headed the ranking in a different product, so that this attribute cannot determine the selection for the group as a whole.
1980: Lightness measures the degree to which the product has remained pale. It declines with browning and with the inward migration of pigments, so that a higher value generally denotes gentler processing. For popped rice the values lay between 64.32 and 72.78, with the control at 69.97; 4 cultivars exceeded the control, Kataribhog ranking highest among them. In puffed rice the values ranged from 67.79 in Tulaipanji to 75.51 in Kataribhog; against the control at 72.23, 4 cultivars ranked higher, Kataribhog being the highest. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 77.35 and Kalojira the lowest at 69.63; against 77.35 for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. The data are presented in Table 4.85 and plotted in Fig. 4.46.
1981: The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. The year effect was significant in 2 products, but the interaction was non-significant throughout, so that the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.04 and 0.39%, attesting to the precision of the trial. Lightness declines as browning products accumulate and as pericarp pigments dissolve and migrate inward; cultivars richer in reducing sugar and free amino nitrogen brown further under an identical treatment.
1982: Comparable observations appear in the literature. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated that darkening proceeds from pigment migration and browning, and Srisang et al. (2021) determined that lightness declines as the thermal treatment becomes more severe. Panda et al. (2021) reported that shorter heating yields a lighter product at equivalent moisture loss, and Akter et al. (2025) observed that a darker product was nonetheless preferred overall. No single cultivar proved superior across all the products: Dudeshwar and Kataribhog ranked highest in different ones, so that the decision is contingent upon the product concerned.
1989: The a* value is signed: a positive value places the sample on the red side of the green-to-red axis and a negative value on the green side. Redness increases as browning proceeds, so that a lower value is preferred. In popped rice the values ranged from -1.86 in Radhatilak to 1.47 in Tulaipanji; the control recorded -0.90, 2 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhatilak returned the most favourable value. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.55 and Harinakhuri the lowest at -1.40; against -0.72 for the control, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, Harinakhuri being the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between -1.03 and 1.50, with the control at -0.53; 3 cultivars exceeded the control and Harinakhuri ranked first. Table 4.86 lists the means and Fig. 4.47 presents them graphically. All the products exhibited a significant cultivar effect. The year effect was significant in 1 product, but the interaction was non-significant throughout, so that the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from -4.61 to 11.92%, indicating good experimental precision.
1990: Redness rises as melanoidins and their coloured precursors accumulate, the rate being contingent upon the reducing sugars and free amino acids the cultivar supplies. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded that the amber shift proceeds from Maillard browning, and Srisang et al. (2021) demonstrated that colour develops with time and temperature. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) noted that the extent of colour development is cultivar-specific, and Panda et al. (2021) concluded that shorter heating restricts colour development.
1991: The most favourable entry varied between products: Harinakhuri and Radhatilak each ranked highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.
1998: Yellowness arises from the migration of bran pigments into the endosperm and from early browning products. Except where a golden colour is required, a lower value is preferable. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in popped rice at 114.00 and Tulaipanji the lowest at 101.07; the control recorded 108.11, 4 cultivars exceeded it and Tulaipanji ranked most favourable. For puffed rice the values lay between 6.13 and 12.09, with the control at 8.65; here 3 cultivars exceeded the control, Radhatilak ranking highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 7.62 in Tulaipanji to 11.62 in Kalonunia; the control returned 9.49, 5 cultivars exceeded that value and Tulaipanji ranked first. The means are given in Table 4.87 and plotted in Fig. 4.48.
